records.sourceFile: Revised Approach to the Role of Fatigue in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Prevention- A Systematic Review with Meta‑Analyses.pdf

paper.citation: Benjaminse A, Webster KE, Kimp A, Meijer M, Gokeler A. Revised Approach to the Role of Fatigue in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Prevention: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analyses. Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: This review pooled laboratory studies that measured lower-limb movement before and after a fatigue protocol during single-leg tasks in healthy people. Fatigue changed only a few variables, mostly in the sagittal plane. The authors argue that fatigue should be part of ACL injury prevention and that current fatigue protocols may be too simple.
paper.tldr: Fatigue changed landing and cutting mechanics in a few sagittal-plane variables in healthy participants, and most variables were not affected. Training under fatigue is worth considering for ACL prevention, but the review does not show that fatigue causes ACL injury.
paper.methods: Three databases were searched up to November 2017. Twenty studies with 3D kinematic or kinetic data before and after a fatigue protocol were included, 18 of them in the meta-analyses, and random-effects pooled effects were calculated where at least three samples were available.
paper.findings: No significant overall effect was found for the single-leg drop vertical jump, and frontal-plane effects were not significant. Knee flexion at initial contact was smaller after fatigue in the single-leg hop for distance and sidestep cutting, and peak knee and hip flexion were greater after fatigue in the single-leg drop landing.
paper.limitations: Studies were laboratory based with small samples, used varied fatigue protocols and peak-angle definitions, and rarely measured performance. The Results section gives the peak hip flexion effect size in the single-leg drop landing as -0.48, while the Discussion gives -0.56, and the abstract attributes the peak-angle changes to the single-leg drop jump rather than the drop landing; the Results values are used here. Few studies used unanticipated tasks.
paper.practicalImplications: Fatigue-based training with sport-specific open skills, such as responding to a cue during a cut or landing, can be one part of a multifactorial ACL prevention program. Fatigue protocols should be chosen with care, because the review suggests current laboratory protocols may not reflect fatigue during play.
paper.athleteDev: Training to resist fatigue with open, sport-specific skills can be included in ACL prevention programs. Fatigue should be monitored alongside workload and aerobic fitness, as the authors propose.
paper.rtp: This review does not provide evidence for return-to-sport decisions. It tested only healthy participants, with no injured or post-ACL reconstruction athletes.

records.sourceFile: Risk Reduction of Concussion in Athletes - Do Neck Size or Neck Strength Make a Difference.pdf

paper.citation: Silverman S, Vidt ME, Hong JS, Grafton LM. Risk Reduction of Concussion in Athletes: Do Neck Size or Neck Strength Make a Difference? Am J Phys Med Rehabil. 2024.
paper.abstract: This narrative review asks whether neck size or neck strength is related to a lower risk of sport-related concussion. Isometric neck strength has more supporting evidence than neck size, and short neck-strengthening programs can raise neck strength. The authors conclude that cervical strengthening is feasible and may help reduce concussion risk, but the best dose is not yet known.
paper.tldr: Neck strength, not neck size, is linked to lower concussion risk, and short neck-strengthening programs can raise neck strength. Evidence that these programs reduce concussions is limited, so they are an option to consider rather than a proven prevention method.
paper.methods: Ovid MEDLINE (13 articles) and Google Scholar (485 results after a pre-2000 filter, 20 retained) were searched with defined key terms. Thirty-three articles on sport-related concussion and neck size or strength were included regardless of sport, sex or age, with screening done by the primary author.
paper.findings: Neck circumference has not been shown to relate to concussion history or future concussion. Isometric neck strength is the better-supported factor, and balance between neck flexor and extensor strength matters. Several strengthening programs increased neck strength, and one high-school football study reported fewer concussions after its program than in the two prior seasons.
paper.limitations: The studies are few and small, the review pools no data, no quality appraisal is described, and the optimal dose is unknown. The authors note that sex-specific and competition-level evidence is limited, and that the benefit may be greater for amateur than professional athletes. The abstract states that programs 'lead to decreased SRC risk', which is stronger than the supporting studies described in the text.
paper.practicalImplications: Simple isometric neck exercises, such as self-resisted holds taking about 3 minutes, are feasible for athletes and could be added to existing training, especially for amateurs and female athletes. Neck strength testing could support screening, but the authors note that dynamometers can be costly, and neck size alone should not be used as a protective measure.
paper.athleteDev: Include isometric neck strengthening with attention to flexor and extensor balance, since neck strength is the factor linked to concussion risk and simple programs can raise it.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the review addresses primary prevention in healthy athletes, not recovery after concussion. It cannot be used to decide when an athlete can return after a concussion.

records.sourceFile: Risk and prognosis of hamstring injuries in the National Football League - A 12-year review.pdf

paper.citation: Jenkins R, Bianchi J, Watson J, Shinners J, Jaisinghani P, Spain B, et al. Risk and Prognosis of Hamstring Injuries in the National Football League: A 12-Year Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2024;12(12):23259671241298622.
paper.abstract: This descriptive study used public NFL injury report data to examine hamstring injuries over 12 seasons. About one third of players were reinjured, and team-level injury rates varied widely. The authors suggest further research into why preventive measures and treatment protocols differ between organizations.
paper.tldr: NFL hamstring injuries kept players on the injury report about 2.4 weeks on average, and about one third of injured players were reinjured. Staff should plan for reinjury risk, but this database cannot explain why some teams have more injuries.
paper.methods: Weekly NFL injury report listings for hamstring injuries were extracted from the public NFL database for 12 seasons. Time on the injury report, practice and game status, position, team rates and reinjury were summarized with descriptive statistics, t tests and chi-square tests.
paper.findings: There were 2101 hamstring injuries in 1354 players, and 442 players (33%) had a reinjury. Defensive skill players accounted for 50.4% of listings, and linebackers had the highest share at 20.1%. Previous injury was not associated with a longer time on the injury report.
paper.limitations: Only in-season listings were used, preseason injuries are not in the database, and tear severity, imaging and treatment are not reported. Data come from elite players with dedicated rehabilitation staff. The overall mean time on the report is given as 2.4 weeks, while the initial-injury value in the reinjury comparison is 2.2 weeks.
paper.practicalImplications: Expect a substantial share of players with a hamstring injury to be reinjured, and build reinjury monitoring into rehabilitation and return-to-play planning. Team-level differences should prompt a review of prevention and treatment practices rather than be taken as proof of what works.
paper.athleteDev: Skill-position players, especially linebackers, wide receivers and cornerbacks, made up most hamstring listings, so they are a priority group for tracking hamstring injury history. The study does not test any prevention program.
paper.rtp: The average time on the injury report was 2.4 weeks, and previous injury was not linked to a longer absence. The study does not test return-to-play criteria or show that any return timing reduces reinjury, so it should not set return timelines on its own.

records.sourceFile: Risk factors for acute ankle sprains in field-based, team contact sports - A systematic review of prospective etiological studies.pdf

paper.citation: Dolan P, Kenny I, Glynn L, Campbell M, Warrington GD, Cahalan R, et al. Risk Factors for Acute Ankle Sprains in Field-Based, Team Contact Sports: a Systematic Review of Prospective Etiological Studies. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: This systematic review identified prospectively measured ankle sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports. Seventeen studies met the criteria, and 12 risk-factor categories were associated with ankle sprain incidence. The authors suggest that BMI, ankle strength, hip strength and single-leg landing performance be considered in athlete assessment, and call for standardized injury definitions.
paper.tldr: Ankle strength, hip strength, BMI and single-leg landing performance were linked to ankle sprain risk across team sports, but the evidence is thin and inconsistent. Use these measures in screening with awareness of the limits, and record injuries with standard definitions.
paper.methods: Eight databases were searched for prospective studies of ankle sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports. Study quality was rated with a modified CASP checklist, and data were extracted from the 17 included studies.
paper.findings: Twelve risk factors were associated with ankle sprain incidence, including anatomic alignment of the foot and ankle, joint laxity, height, mass, BMI, age, ankle strength, hip strength, single-leg landing performance and single-leg reach. Deficits or asymmetries in ankle strength and hip strength were each associated in two studies.
paper.limitations: Only the accepted author version was available, so pagination is missing. Injury definitions and diagnosis varied, only seven of 17 studies reported an incidence rate, and only four studied women. Several associations come from single studies, and the BMI findings conflict across studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Ankle and hip strength, BMI and single-leg landing performance can be included in athlete assessment as the authors suggest, with the thin evidence base in mind. Measuring these in a standardized way across seasons would make results more useful.
paper.athleteDev: Use ankle and hip strength tests and single-leg landing and reach screening as part of athlete assessment and program design, as the review proposes. Record injuries with standard definitions so findings can be checked locally.
paper.rtp: The review concerns the risk of ankle sprain measured from preseason baselines. It does not inform return-to-play decisions after an ankle sprain.

records.sourceFile: Risk factors for hamstring muscle injury in male elite football - Medical expert experience and conclusions from 15 European Champions League cl.pdf

paper.citation: Ekstrand J, Ueblacker P, Van Zoest W, Verheijen R, Vanhecke B, van Wijk M, et al. Risk factors for hamstring muscle injury in male elite football: medical expert experience and conclusions from 15 European Champions League clubs. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2023;9:e001461.
paper.abstract: Chief medical officers of 15 European professional clubs suggested and rated hamstring injury risk factors. Most were extrinsic, linked to coaching, team or club. Clubs with higher hamstring injury burden rated fatigue, wellness and coach leadership style as more important than clubs with lower burden.
paper.tldr: Club medical officers rate communication between medical and coaching staff and high-speed training exposure as the most important hamstring risk factors, and most of the factors they name are controlled by coaching staff. The study shows clinicians' beliefs, not proven causes.
paper.methods: Chief medical officers of 15 clubs completed an online questionnaire. They first named risk factors, then rated each on a 5-point scale, and ratings were compared between clubs with lower and higher than average hamstring injury burden using weighted averages.
paper.findings: Twenty-one risk factors were suggested, with 12 extrinsic and nine intrinsic. Compared with the low-burden group, the high-burden group rated fatigue (3.6 vs 2.6), player wellness (3.0 vs 2.0) and coach leadership style (3.3 vs 2.1) as more important. The low-burden group rated lack of high-speed training higher (3.8 vs 3.5).
paper.limitations: Findings rest on expert opinion from 15 clubs, with only two seasons of injury data used to form the groups. The authors note the study design cannot show causality, and other club differences that were not measured may explain the injury rates.
paper.practicalImplications: Clubs can review how medical and coaching staff communicate about load and fatigue, and how much high-speed running is included in training, since these were rated most important. The study does not show that changing these factors reduces hamstring injury.
paper.athleteDev: Medical officers rated regular high-speed running exposure and joint load decisions between coaching and medical staff as most important, and higher-burden clubs rated fatigue and player wellness higher. These are expert ratings, and the study does not test whether acting on them lowers hamstring injury.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return-to-play decisions, because the study covers risk factors for hamstring injury rather than recovery. It rates residual weakness after a previous hamstring injury as an important risk factor, but it does not test return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Risk of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tears in National Football League Players by Short, Normal, or Long Rest Weeks.pdf

paper.citation: Garlapaty A, Scheiderer JA, Rucinski K, DeFroda SF. Risk of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tears in National Football League Players by Short, Normal, or Long Rest Weeks. Journal of Knee Surgery. 2024.
paper.abstract: ACL tears in NFL players are season-ending injuries, and deviation from the usual 7-day rest week between games has been proposed as a risk factor. The authors classified 220 publicly reported regular-season ACL tears from 2012-2013 to 2022-2023 as short, normal or long week injuries. They report that players were 1.8 times more likely to tear their ACL in a long week and 1.5 times more likely in a short week than in a normal week.
paper.tldr: In this public-data study of NFL players, ACL tears were more common in weeks with a short or long gap between games than in normal 7-day weeks. Because the analysis is unadjusted, use it to flag schedule weeks for closer knee-injury monitoring, not as proof of a cause.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of publicly reported ACL tears in NFL regular-season games, with each tear coded by the interval since the player's previous game. Fisher's exact, chi-square and one-way ANOVA tests were used, with p<.05 as the threshold.
paper.findings: Of 220 included tears, 24 occurred in short weeks, 128 in normal weeks and 68 in long weeks. The authors report tear rates of 0.030, 0.037 and 0.048 per game for short, normal and long weeks. Position, age, BMI, experience, playing surface and contact mechanism were not significantly associated with week length.
paper.limitations: Injury and timing data came from public sources, so some injuries may be missing, and days between games may not reflect actual rest or recovery. The reported ratios do not match the reported rates: the short-week rate (0.030) is below the normal-week rate (0.037), and the long-week rate (0.048) is about 1.3 times normal, not 1.8. One version of the abstract also describes a 6-day rest week, while the methods use 7 days.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who plan around short or long game gaps may use this to review knee-injury risk and player readiness in those weeks. The study cannot say which rest pattern is safer or whether changing the schedule would reduce ACL tears.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured only days between games and no training load, so it cannot guide how to program training around short or long weeks. Performance staff should track their own load and readiness data before changing the weekly plan.
paper.rtp: The study measures injury incidence, not recovery, so it cannot inform return-to-sport timing, criteria or readiness decisions.

records.sourceFile: Risk of concussion after a targeting foul in collegiate American football.pdf

paper.citation: Aukerman DF, Bohr AD, Poddar SK, Romano R, Petron DJ, Ghajar J, et al. Risk of Concussion After a Targeting Foul in Collegiate American Football. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;10(2):23259671221074656.
paper.abstract: The study compared concussion incidence between Pac-12 football plays where a targeting penalty was called and all other plays across 538 games from 2016 to 2019. Incidence was 106.4 per 1000 plays on targeting plays versus 2.9 per 1000 on other plays, a risk ratio of 36.9 (95% CI, 22.4-60.7), and 49.0 when only upheld targeting calls were counted. The authors conclude that concussion risk was significantly higher on targeting plays, especially upheld ones.
paper.tldr: Concussions were far more common on Pac-12 plays where a targeting penalty was called than on other plays. The sample is small and from one conference, so the finding supports screening players after a targeting play, not a precise national rate.
paper.methods: Concussion counts from athletic training records for all Pac-12 games in 2016-2019 were sorted into upheld targeting, overturned targeting and all other plays, with targeting plays checked by the authors on video. Incidence per 1000 plays and risk ratios with 95% CIs were calculated, and position and play type were described for 2018 and 2019.
paper.findings: Of 213 concussions, 15 occurred on targeting plays (12 upheld, 3 overturned) and 198 on other plays. Incidence was 141.2 per 1000 plays for upheld calls and 53.6 per 1000 for overturned calls, against 2.9 per 1000 for other plays. The risk ratio was 36.9 for all targeting plays and 49.0 for upheld calls versus other plays, while upheld versus overturned (RR 2.6, 95% CI 0.8-8.9) was not statistically significant. Passing plays accounted for 59.0% of targeting penalties, and offensive players or kick/punt returners were the targeted player on 72 of 78 calls in 2018-2019.
paper.limitations: The study covers one conference, so it may not generalize to all NCAA programs. It did not measure whether targeting penalties deter contact or compare concussion rates before the 2008 rule, and the deidentified data prevented comparing targeted and targeting players. The estimate of 387 concussions across Division I is an extrapolation from the same 15 events and an estimated penalty count.
paper.practicalImplications: Medical staff covering college football could screen players involved in a targeting play for concussion, even when the penalty is overturned, as the authors advise. The data do not show that removing targeting would reduce concussions.
paper.athleteDev: Coaches can use the finding to stress tackling and blocking technique that avoids head contact, the behavior targeting rules aim to reduce. The study does not measure technique or training, so it cannot show which drills reduce targeting.
paper.rtp: The study counts concussions by play type and does not address recovery, so it cannot inform return-to-play timing or criteria.

records.sourceFile: Risk of upper extremity musculoskeletal injury within the first year after a concussion.pdf

paper.citation: Roach MH, Aderman MJ, Ross JD, Kelly TF, Malvasi SR, Posner MA, et al. Risk of Upper Extremity Musculoskeletal Injury Within the First Year After a Concussion. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;11(5):23259671231163570.
paper.abstract: The study examined whether concussion is associated with acute upper-extremity musculoskeletal injury in the 12 months after unrestricted return to activity. Among 316 concussed cadets matched to 316 nonconcussed controls, 19.3% of concussed and 9.2% of control participants sustained an upper-extremity injury. The concussed group had a higher hazard of injury after adjustment (HR 1.84), with varsity sport level also an independent risk factor.
paper.tldr: Cadets who had a concussion sustained more upper-extremity musculoskeletal injuries than matched peers in the following year (unadjusted HR 2.25, adjusted HR 1.84). Staff can watch shoulder, arm and hand injuries after concussion, but the study does not explain why the risk is higher.
paper.methods: Nested case-control design within the prospective CARE Consortium cohort at the US Military Academy, with 316 concussed cadets matched by sex and sport level to 316 nonconcussed controls. Upper-extremity injuries were tracked for 12 months after unrestricted return to activity, and Cox proportional hazards models were fitted unadjusted and adjusted for sport level, concussion history, BSI-18 somatization and prior upper-extremity injury.
paper.findings: Upper-extremity injury occurred in 19.3% (61/316) of concussed and 9.2% (29/316) of control participants during follow-up. The unadjusted HR was 2.25 (95% CI, 1.45-3.51) and the adjusted HR was 1.84 (95% CI, 1.10-3.07, P=.019). Varsity sport level was an independent risk factor (adjusted HR 2.53), while concussion history, somatization and prior upper-extremity injury were not significant after adjustment. Shoulder injuries were the most common upper-extremity injury in both groups.
paper.limitations: Participants were US Military Academy cadets, so the results may not transfer to other athletes or civilians. Training exposure was not captured, injuries not reported to a medical provider would be missed, and concussion history was self-reported. The abstract's 'more than twice as likely' conclusion uses the unadjusted HR, the methods describe a nested case-control design although the abstract calls it a cohort study, and the Discussion gives a univariate HR of 2.25 for prior UE injury where Table 2 reports 1.84.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians managing concussed athletes can warn them and their staff that upper-extremity injuries were more common in the year after return to activity, with shoulder injuries the most frequent type. The study does not show that any screening or program prevents these injuries.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff may watch shoulder, elbow and hand injury risk in the year after a concussion, since these injuries were more frequent in concussed cadets. The study tested no training intervention and cannot say which program would reduce that risk.
paper.rtp: The study follows athletes after unrestricted return to activity and shows a higher injury risk in the following year, which is relevant to monitoring after return. It does not assess return-to-play criteria, timing or clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Role of Hip Internal Rotation Range and Foot Progression Angle for Preventing Jones Fracture During Crossover Cutting.pdf

paper.citation: Kikuchi Y, Takabayashi T, Kikumoto T, Watanabe T, Suzuki S, Hiratsuka S, et al. Role of Hip Internal Rotation Range and Foot Progression Angle for Preventing Jones Fracture During Crossover Cutting. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2024. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: The study examined how passive and dynamic hip internal rotation range and foot progression angle (FPA) relate to force on the fifth metatarsal during 45-degree crossover cutting in 20 male college soccer players. Hip internal rotation was not correlated with M5 force, while greater FPA was correlated with lower M5 force (r=-.56, P<.01). The authors conclude that minimizing FPA reduces M5 pressure and could prevent Jones fracture, a statement that conflicts with their reported correlation.
paper.tldr: In 20 male college soccer players, a larger foot progression angle at foot contact during 45-degree crossover cuts went with lower force on the fifth metatarsal, while hip rotation range did not. This is a laboratory correlation, not evidence that changing foot angle prevents Jones fractures.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional laboratory study. Passive hip internal rotation was measured in the prone position, and 3D motion capture, force plates and Footscan plates recorded dynamic hip rotation, FPA and peak force on the M5 across five barefoot 45-degree crossover cuts. Pearson correlations were used to relate the variables.
paper.findings: Passive hip internal rotation averaged 39.9 degrees and dynamic hip internal rotation 5.8 degrees, and neither was correlated with M5 force (P>.05). FPA at initial contact (mean 29.7 degrees) was negatively correlated with M5 force (r=-.56, P<.01), as were lower leg external rotation (r=-.56, P<.01) and thigh external rotation (r=-.54, P<.05).
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot establish that the angles cause Jones fractures, and no fracture cases were studied. Force was taken from the Footscan M5 zone rather than the bending moment, and the task was a single 45-degree cut, barefoot, in a laboratory, with 20 men. The abstract's conclusion that minimizing FPA reduces M5 pressure conflicts with its own negative correlation and with the Discussion, which recommends increasing FPA; this summary follows the reported results. The abstract also calls the outcome plantar pressure, while the results report peak force in %BW.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could consider cueing a larger foot angle toward the new direction during 45-degree cuts as a lab-based hypothesis for lower M5 load. The study measured only correlation and no injury outcome, so any cueing should be treated as untested.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff working on change-of-direction with soccer players can assess FPA during crossover cuts, since FPA was among the variables most strongly tied to lower M5 force here. Any technique cue should be checked against loading data in training rather than assumed to reduce risk.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy players and no rehabilitation or clearance measure, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions after a Jones fracture. It also does not show that changing FPA reduces refracture risk.

records.sourceFile: Running exposure is associated with the risk of hamstring strain injury in elite Australian footballers.pdf

paper.citation: Ruddy JD, Pollard CW, Timmins RG, Williams MD, Shield AJ, Opar DA. Running exposure is associated with the risk of hamstring strain injury in elite Australian footballers. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52:919-928.
paper.abstract: The study examined whether GPS running exposure is associated with hamstring strain injury (HSI) in the following week among 220 elite Australian footballers from five teams during the 2015 season. Weekly distance above 24 km/h greater than 653 m was associated with a relative risk of 3.4 (95% CI 1.6 to 7.2), and distance above 24 km/h as a percentage of distance above 10 km/h greater than 2.5% with a relative risk of 6.3 (95% CI 1.5 to 26.7). The authors conclude that the associations are present but that the predictive capacity of running exposure variables is limited.
paper.tldr: Elite Australian footballers who covered more distance at high speed in a week had a higher chance of a hamstring strain the following week, but the cut-points were too imprecise to pick out individual players. Treat GPS running load as one input to hamstring risk management, not a stand-alone screen.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort study across the 2015 AFL season, using GPS data from every training session and match for players from five of six approached clubs. Weekly absolute and relative running variables for distance above 10 and 24 km/h were compared with MRI-confirmed hamstring injuries in the following week, using ROC analysis to set cut-points and relative risks with 95% CIs.
paper.findings: Of 220 players, 30 sustained a prospective HSI, 28 of them in biceps femoris, and high-speed running was the primary mechanism (53%). Weekly distance above 24 km/h greater than 653 m (RR 3.4, sensitivity 0.52, specificity 0.76, AUC 0.63) and the 24 km/h share above 2.5% (RR 6.3, sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.34, AUC 0.63) had the largest significant associations. Previous HSI (RR 2.0, 95% CI 0.9 to 4.2) and age were not significantly associated with injury. In the worked example, the post-test probability for weekly distance above 24 km/h greater than 653 m was 0.9%, against a pre-test probability of 0.4%.
paper.limitations: The sample came from five teams in one season, and the raw GPS files had no activity periods, so total distance and low-speed or recovery sessions were not analyzed. Athlete-weeks were the unit of analysis, which precluded a multivariable model, and several cut-points were derived from ROC curves on the same data. The conclusion that the association is strongest within a 7-14 day window partly draws on an earlier study cited by the authors.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners tracking GPS running exposure can use the high-speed distance markers as descriptive flags, but the authors stress that their predictive value is too low to use alone. The markers fit within broader hamstring risk-mitigation strategies rather than replacing them.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can track weekly distance above 24 km/h and large week-to-week changes in it, since larger values preceded next-week hamstring strain in this cohort. Because most flagged weeks were not followed by injury, these markers should not set training limits by themselves.
paper.rtp: The study tracks who is injured, not recovery, so it cannot guide return-to-play timing or loading after a hamstring strain. Its running-exposure markers have limited predictive value, so they do not settle return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: SARS-CoV-2 infection increases the risk of muscle injury in professional male soccer players - A retrospective analysis of the Italian and Spani.pdf

paper.citation: Miccinilli S, Bravi M, Conti G, Bressi F, Sterzi S, Santacaterina F, et al. SARS-CoV-2 Infection Increases the Risk of Muscle Injury in Professional Male Soccer Players: A Retrospective Analysis of the Italian and Spanish Major Leagues. Infect Dis Rep. 2023;15:425-435.
paper.abstract: Retrospective cohort of 1,283 male players in Serie A and LaLiga over two seasons, comparing players who had SARS-CoV-2 in 2020-21 with those who did not, using muscle injury counts from a public database.
paper.tldr: Professional footballers who had COVID-19 in the 2020-21 season had about three to five times the hazard of muscle injury that season. The authors argue infection should be treated as a return-to-play concern that needs specific assessment.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort of Serie A and LaLiga players, using Transfermarkt injury, match and minute data. Players were grouped by infection in 2020-21 and compared with t tests, multiple linear regression and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, following STROBE and CHAMP guidance.
paper.findings: In 2020-21, infected players had more muscle injuries than uninfected players (Serie A 1.44 vs 0.56; LaLiga 1.23 vs 0.32), with hazard ratios of 3.73 (95% CI 3.018 to 4.628) in Serie A and 5.14 (95% CI 3.200 to 8.254) in LaLiga. The two groups did not differ significantly in 2019-20.
paper.limitations: Injury data came from a single database and may have over- or under-counted events. Prior injuries, COVID severity, quarantine length and injured body part were not controlled, and injury type was not recorded, so no subanalysis was possible.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest infection history should be part of return-to-play decisions, with specific muscle assessment and training rather than only symptom resolution. They call for further study of tailored rehabilitation after infection.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Staff should consider infection status alongside workload when reading muscle injury risk in a season when a player has had COVID-19. The paper reports no performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The authors recommend that return-to-play decisions after SARS-CoV-2 include specific muscle assessment and training, not only symptom remission and drug cessation. The study cannot set a return-to-play timeline or show that these steps reduce injury.

records.sourceFile: Same-year repeat concussions in the National Football League - Trends from 2015-through 2019.pdf

paper.citation: Cools M, Zuckerman S, Herzog M, Mack C, Lee RY, Solomon G, et al. Same-Year Repeat Concussions in the National Football League: Trends from 2015 through 2019. World Neurosurgery. 2022.
paper.abstract: Retrospective study of NFL concussions in 2015 to 2019 that measured the risk of a second concussion in the same NFL year, the time between injuries and return-to-play time.
paper.tldr: Among NFL players who had a concussion, the chance of a second one in the same NFL year was about the same as any player's chance of a first. Repeat concussions were followed by longer time out, and about 1 in 5 repeats came within two weeks of return.
paper.methods: Retrospective observational cohort of all NFL players with concussions in 2015 to 2019, drawn from the league's electronic health records. Rates were calculated per season, missed and participation days were compared with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, and risk ratios were estimated with log-binomial regression.
paper.findings: Same-year repeat concussion occurred in 0.38% to 0.69% of all players per season and in 5.3% to 8.3% of concussed players, similar to the one-season risk of any concussion among all players (6.2% to 8.3%). The median number of participation days between injuries was 38, and 18.8% of repeats occurred within two weeks of return. Median missed time was 12 days after a repeat concussion, against 9 days after a single concussion (p less than 0.0001).
paper.limitations: Single-league data with no player-exposure denominator and no account of limits set after clearance. Few repeat events limited subgroup analysis. The abstract calls the design case-control while the Methods describe a cohort. The Discussion gives a single-concussion range of 6.2% to 8.0%, against 6.2% to 8.3% in Table 1. The Conclusion links more missed time to higher repeat risk, but the reported result (RR 1.48, 95% CI 0.94 to 2.31) was not significant. The comparator for the repeat risk is the risk of any concussion among all players, and no formal test of that comparison is shown in the Results. Two authors are affiliated with the NFL.
paper.practicalImplications: Players cleared under the current protocols had a same-year repeat risk similar to the league-wide risk of a first concussion. Longer missed time after a first concussion may warrant closer review, though the association was not significant.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The paper does not measure performance. Its use is in planning season-level risk and availability after concussion.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Cleared players had a same-year repeat risk similar to the league-wide risk of any concussion, which is consistent with, but does not prove, adequate recovery before return under staged protocols. The study has no comparison protocol and cannot show cause, and longer missed time after a first concussion may warrant closer review.

records.sourceFile: Sciatic Nerve Conductivity is Impaired by Hamstring Strain Injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Kouzaki K, Nakazato K, Mizuno M, Yonechi T, Higo Y, Kubo Y, et al. Sciatic Nerve Conductivity is Impaired by Hamstring Strain Injuries. Int J Sports Med. 2017;38:803-808.
paper.abstract: Twenty-seven athletes with a history of hamstring strain injury were compared with 16 uninjured controls, using magnetic stimulation of the sciatic nerve. In the injured athletes, the injured limb had longer latencies and slower nerve conduction velocity than the uninjured limb, while controls showed no side-to-side difference. The authors suggest sciatic nerve conductivity may be impaired after hamstring strain.
paper.tldr: Athletes with a past hamstring strain showed slower sciatic nerve conduction in the injured leg than in the uninjured leg. Controls showed no side-to-side difference.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional group comparison. Twenty-seven athletes with a non-traumatic hamstring injury history (acute or chronic) were compared with 16 uninjured recreational controls. Proximal and distal M-wave latencies and sciatic nerve conduction velocity were measured by magnetic stimulation at two sites, with MRI used to check for signal change at the injury. Non-parametric tests were used, with side-to-side and between-group comparisons.
paper.findings: In the injured group, proximal latency and distal latency were longer in the injured limb than the uninjured limb (both P<0.05). Nerve conduction velocity was 64.5 m/s in the injured limb versus 76.4 m/s in the uninjured limb (P<0.05). Relative proximal latency difference was 13% in the injured group versus 3% in controls, and relative nerve conduction velocity was 84% versus 98%. MRI showed high signal in 10 of 27 injured athletes.
paper.limitations: The sample was small (27 injured, 16 controls) and cross-sectional, with time since injury ranging from 1 to 70 months. The injured site and damage severity were not examined. The controls were less active than the athletes. The authors also note the reliability of the significant findings is uncertain given the sample size.
paper.practicalImplications: The study links a past hamstring strain with slower sciatic nerve conduction in the injured leg, measured months to years after injury. It cannot show that nerve testing changes management, because it did not follow athletes over time or measure re-injury.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the study suggests only that a past hamstring strain may be associated with slower sciatic nerve conduction in the injured leg. It does not support using this measure to monitor or train athletes.
paper.rtp: This cross-sectional study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Athletes were tested 1 to 70 months after injury, so it does not show how nerve conduction changes during recovery or whether it should guide the timing of return to play.

records.sourceFile: Sciatic nerve compression after a chronic proximal hamstring tear - A report of two cases and a narrative review of the literature.pdf

paper.citation: Gattringer M, Schalamon G, Pichler H, Breulmann FL, Buerger H, Mattiassich G, et al. Sciatic Nerve Compression after a Chronic Proximal Hamstring Tear: A Report of Two Cases and a Narrative Review of the Literature. Life. 2023;13:1762.
paper.abstract: Two patients with chronic proximal hamstring tears and sciatic nerve compression, initially treated conservatively at another institution, underwent open sciatic neurolysis. Neurological symptoms improved after surgery in both, although the second patient kept some symptoms for up to a year. Neither patient had the ruptured muscles reattached to the ischial tuberosity; in the second case the biceps femoris was sutured to the semimembranosus over the nerve. The authors suggest that neurolysis without reattachment is an applicable option for chronic tears with sciatic compression, pending further study.
paper.tldr: Two patients with chronic hamstring tears and sciatic nerve compression improved after nerve release. One returned to sport within weeks, while the other had weakness and pain on sitting for up to a year.
paper.methods: Case report of two patients treated at one institution, with a narrative review of the literature on proximal hamstring tears and sciatic nerve compression. Both patients were treated conservatively first, and then underwent microscopic neurolysis of the sciatic nerve. Outcomes were described from clinical history, MRI, intraoperative findings and follow-up.
paper.findings: Case 1: symptoms and giving way improved by 4 weeks after surgery, return to sport occurred several weeks later, and the patient was free of complaints at 2 years. Case 2: giving way and shooting pain resolved over weeks, while strength deficit, paresthesia and posterior thigh pain on sitting persisted for up to one year. Electromyography and tibial nerve conduction studies in case 2 were normal before surgery.
paper.limitations: Only two cases, with no standardized outcome measures and no control group. Follow-up was 2 years in one case and about 1 year for persistent symptoms in the other. The narrative review does not describe a search method, and the authors note that no evidence exists on optimal treatment.
paper.practicalImplications: When sciatic symptoms persist after a chronic proximal hamstring tear, the authors propose open neurolysis without reattaching the torn muscles to the ischial tuberosity as an applicable option, a hypothesis they say needs further study. Patients may still have weakness, paresthesia or pain on sitting for up to a year after surgery, as the second case shows.
paper.athleteDev: This report gives no training or performance guidance. Its relevance is limited to recognizing that persistent posterior thigh pain and giving-way after a proximal hamstring tear can signal nerve involvement that needs medical review before an athlete returns to training.
paper.rtp: Two cases cannot set a return-to-sport timeline or show that neurolysis is needed for return to play. Case 1 returned to sport several weeks after surgery, while case 2 had residual weakness and pain on sitting for up to a year, and the report does not state a formal return-to-sport protocol.

records.sourceFile: Screening hamstring injury risk factors multiple times in a season does not improve the identification of future injury risk.pdf

paper.citation: Opar DA, Ruddy JD, Williams MD, Maniar N, Hickey JT, Bourne MN, et al. Screening Hamstring Injury Risk Factors Multiple Times in a Season Does Not Improve the Identification of Future Injury Risk. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, published ahead of print, 2021.
paper.abstract: A prospective cohort of 311 Australian Football players (455 player seasons) was assessed for eccentric knee flexor strength and biceps femoris long head architecture once or repeatedly in a season. Prior hamstring injury was the strongest risk factor; shorter absolute fascicle length and between-limb strength imbalance were associated with injury only when measured repeatedly, while shorter relative fascicle length was associated at both frequencies. Repeated testing did not meaningfully improve prediction, and the authors conclude that frequent measurement of these variables does not improve identification of future injury.
paper.tldr: Testing hamstring risk factors several times a season did not identify injuries better than a single preseason test. A prior hamstring injury was the most useful predictor, and prediction was only modest.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort across the 2018 and 2019 AFL regular seasons with six teams. Eccentric knee flexor strength was measured with the Nordic hamstring exercise on an instrumented device, and biceps femoris long head fascicle length, pennation angle and muscle thickness were measured by ultrasound at preseason start, preseason end and mid-season. Cut-points were set by ROC analysis, univariable relative risks were calculated, and multivariable logistic models were built with stepwise regression. Model AUCs at single and repeated time points were compared with bootstrapped confidence intervals.
paper.findings: Of 455 player seasons, 74 (16.3%) had an index hamstring injury. Prior hamstring injury was associated with injury (RR 2.85, 95% CI 1.88 to 4.33). At preseason start, relative fascicle length at or below 3.82 (RR 1.78, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.75) and pennation angle above 15.8 (RR 1.78, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.74) were associated with injury. Across repeated measures, absolute fascicle length at or below 10.42 cm (RR 1.89, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.99) and between-limb imbalance (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.06 to 3.08) were associated with injury. Eccentric strength was not associated with injury. The best single-time-point model had AUC 0.681 and the best repeated-measures model had AUC 0.726, with overlapping confidence intervals.
paper.limitations: Single league, male-only sample. Injury muscle was recorded for 66% of injuries and no standard classification was used. Fascicle length was estimated by extrapolation, which may overestimate length. Warm-up was not standardized, and exposure was not reported. The abstract gives the imbalance cut-point as above 9%, the Results as 9% or less, and the Discussion as 9% or more. Several authors report financial ties to Vald Performance, which commercializes the strength testing device.
paper.practicalImplications: Repeating Nordic strength and fascicle length testing across the season did not meaningfully improve injury prediction over a single preseason test, and a prior hamstring injury remained the clearest flag. Repeated testing should therefore be justified by something other than better injury prediction, and the modest discrimination means these measures alone should not decide who is at risk.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, this study suggests that repeated Nordic strength and fascicle testing across a season is not a better injury screen than one preseason test. Its clearest risk signal was a hamstring injury in the previous 12 months, and eccentric strength itself was not associated with injury.
paper.rtp: This cohort study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It examined the risk of an index hamstring injury during a season, not recovery after injury, and it did not test rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Secondary injury prevention reduces hamstring strain and time-loss groin injury burdens in male professional football.pdf

paper.citation: Adams SR, Wollin M, Drew MK, Toohey LA, Smith C, Borges N, et al. Secondary injury prevention reduces hamstring strain and time-loss groin injury burdens in male professional football. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2024.
paper.abstract: Prospective cohort study of 73 male professional football players at one Australian club over five seasons: two control seasons with usual care, then three intervention seasons with a systems-based secondary injury prevention system using post-match isometric knee flexion and hip adduction strength testing. Burdens were compared between periods. HSI burden fell by 4.98 days absence per 1000 h (19.8%) and time-loss groin burden by 3.93 days absence per 1000 h (25.6%) in the intervention period.
paper.tldr: At one professional club, adding post-match strength screening with indicated responses was followed by lower hamstring strain and groin injury burdens than the two previous seasons. The design is a non-randomised comparison with earlier seasons, so this is a preliminary signal rather than proof of effect.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort over five seasons (2016/17 to 2020/21) at one male professional club. The first two seasons were usual care; the next three added testing two days post-match of unilateral knee flexion and side-lying hip adduction maximum voluntary isometric contractions. An alert was raised when a player's strength fell beyond the test's minimal detectable change from their 8-test moving average, and a retest the next day guided physiotherapy, strengthening and load reductions. Incidence rates were compared with Poisson-type regression, and burden (days absence per 1000 player hours) was reported with 95% CIs without a significance test.
paper.findings: HSI burden was 20.20 versus 25.18 days absence per 1000 h (4.98 lower, 19.8%), with match HSI burden down 59.0%; HSI incidence was similar (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.33, p = 0.93). Time-loss groin burden was 11.44 versus 15.37 days per 1000 h (3.93 lower, 25.6%), and groin incidence was lower (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.34, p = 0.17), which was not significant. The intervention period produced 30 strength-reduction alerts for 17 players.
paper.limitations: Non-randomised, with a historical control period and a single club. The abstract reports the groin change as 0.57 days absence per 1000 h (49.1%), but the Results give the burden change as 3.93 days per 1000 h (25.6%); the 49% figure is the drop in incidence (1.16 to 0.59 per 1000 h). Burden differences were not tested statistically and their CIs overlap, and groin injury severity rose (13 to 19 days per injury, p = 0.167) even as burden fell. The authors note a possible lead-time effect and possible staff influence on return-to-play decisions.
paper.practicalImplications: Clubs with a sports-medicine-led process could consider regular post-match isometric strength testing with pre-set alerts, followed by individual load and position-based changes, alongside usual primary and tertiary prevention. The authors advise against using this testing in isolation.
paper.athleteDev: Post-match isometric knee flexion and hip adduction testing, with alerts set against each player's own recent average, can guide training exposure for players whose strength has dropped. Dominant limbs and forwards and wide players were more often flagged in this study.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It did not test return-to-play criteria or outcomes, and the authors note that the boundary between end of time loss and return to play is not objectively clear.

records.sourceFile: Sensitivity and specificity of on-field visible signs of concussion in the National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Elbin RJ, Zuckerman SL, Sills AK, Crandall JR, Lessley DJ, Solomon GS. Sensitivity and Specificity of On-Field Visible Signs of Concussion in the National Football League. Neurosurgery. 2020.
paper.abstract: Video review by two expert raters of 251 NFL injury plays from the 2017 season (211 diagnosed with sport-related concussion, 40 not) using a visible-signs checklist. Slow to get up and motor incoordination were the most frequent signs in concussed players, slow to get up was the most sensitive, and 26% of concussed players showed no visible sign. The checklist had sensitivity of 73%, specificity of 65% and an AUC of 0.66, which the authors call poor, so concussion cannot be diagnosed from visible signs alone.
paper.tldr: In NFL video review, the visible-signs checklist missed about a quarter of diagnosed concussions and had poor overall discrimination (AUC 0.66). Visible signs are one part of the sideline evaluation, not a diagnostic tool on their own.
paper.methods: Prospective observational cross-sectional study using video of injury plays from the 2017 NFL season where a player was removed for suspected concussion. Two expert raters independently scored the AFL visible-signs checklist for each play. Logistic regression tested each sign, and a receiver operating characteristic curve with AUC summarised the checklist. Sensitivity and specificity were calculated against the team physician and neurotrauma consultant's diagnosis.
paper.findings: Concussed players most often showed slow to get up (averaged 65.9%) and motor incoordination (28.4%). In non-concussed players, slow to get up was also most common (60.0%). The checklist had combined sensitivity of 73.46% and specificity of 65.0%, and 26% of concussed players showed no visible sign. Multivariate logistic regression identified motor incoordination (OR 3.96, 95% CI 1.64 to 9.56, P = .002) and loss of responsiveness (OR 5.17, 95% CI 1.14 to 23.42, P = .033) as significant predictors. The AUC was 0.66.
paper.limitations: Two raters, with no third rater to resolve disagreements; only one season; only players removed for suspected concussion were reviewed; and a league-specific checklist. The Discussion states sensitivity and specificity of 76% and 63%, but the Results and Table 5 give 73% and 65% combined, so the Discussion figures should not be quoted. The sign definitions differ from the new consensus list, and several authors are employed by or consult for the NFL.
paper.practicalImplications: Use visible-sign checks as one input to a full sideline or acute evaluation, not as a stand-alone screen. Signs with high specificity, such as loss of responsiveness, may still support removal from play, but the authors call it unacceptable to miss 1 in 4 concussions with visible signs alone, so an absence of signs cannot rule out injury.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable to performance development. The paper is about recognising concussion in games.
paper.rtp: The paper does not inform return to sport. It addresses identification of concussion at the time of injury, and the authors do not test any return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Serial ultrasound imaging leading up to an Achilles tendon rupture after identification of a thickened paratenon.pdf

paper.citation: Ford K, Monson N, Glauser S, Cushman DM. Serial Ultrasound Imaging Leading up to an Achilles Tendon Rupture After Identification of a Thickened Paratenon: A Case Report. American Journal of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation. 2025;104(11):1067-1069.
paper.abstract: A 22-year-old collegiate lacrosse student-athlete had normal Achilles tendons on ultrasound seven months before injury. About four weeks before rupture he developed pain, and repeat ultrasound showed a normal-appearing tendon with new hypoechoic paratenon thickening. He then suffered a complete Achilles rupture. The case is the second known rupture preceded by normal asymptomatic advanced imaging and raises questions about the paratenon's role in rupture.
paper.tldr: A collegiate lacrosse player with a normal Achilles on ultrasound seven months earlier developed new paratenon thickening about two weeks before a complete rupture. One case cannot show whether paratenon thickening predicts rupture, but the authors suggest extra caution when it is seen acutely in explosive athletes.
paper.methods: Single case report following CARE guidelines. The athlete had a research ultrasound of both Achilles tendons seven months before injury, and symptomatic pain prompted a clinical exam and repeat ultrasound about two weeks before rupture. MRI was performed two days after rupture, and surgery was undertaken five days after injury.
paper.findings: At the initial scan, both tendons were normal. Repeat ultrasound about two weeks before rupture showed a normal-appearing tendon with hypoechoic paratenon thickening on the medial superficial surface, 1 to 4 cm above the calcaneus, while the plantaris was intact. The rupture occurred during push-off. MRI showed a complete rupture and severe tendinosis of the remnant distal tendon, which ultrasound had not shown two weeks earlier. The paratenon was not ruptured at surgery.
paper.limitations: One athlete and one case, with only two ultrasound time points before rupture and no histopathology of the tendon or paratenon. Meloxicam was prescribed and new cleats had been introduced, so the paratenon change cannot be attributed to a single cause. The authors note the thickening may have been a normal healing response.
paper.practicalImplications: Acute paratenon thickening on ultrasound in an athlete with Achilles pain may merit closer follow-up, especially in explosive sports, as the authors suggest. The case does not set a threshold for restricting training or for predicting rupture.
paper.athleteDev: Not a performance application. The case links new cleats and conditioning to the onset of pain, but the paper does not establish a cause, so staff should not treat footwear changes as a proven risk.
paper.rtp: The paper gives no return-to-play timeline or criteria; the athlete returned gradually after open repair under a standard protocol. It does not show whether paratenon findings should change return timing, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Shoulder injury patterns and trends in the National Football League - An epidemiological analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Fares MY, Daher M, Boufadel P, Singh J, Bdeir A, Koa J, et al. Shoulder injury patterns and trends in the National Football League: an epidemiological analysis. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2024.
paper.abstract: Injury data from the 2019 to 2022 NFL seasons were extracted from the official NFL injury report and secondary sources. Of 6,732 injuries, 452 (6.7%) were to the shoulder, an injury rate of 4.5 per 1000 athletic exposures. Linebackers, cornerbacks, wide receivers and safeties had significantly more shoulder injuries than several other positions, most injuries were mild (66%), and there was no clear distribution across the season.
paper.tldr: Shoulder injuries made up 6.7% of NFL injuries from 2019 to 2022, and most were mild muscle or ligament injuries. Counts were highest for linebackers, cornerbacks and wide receivers, which the authors suggest may benefit from more targeted protocols.
paper.methods: Descriptive epidemiological study of NFL injury reports for the 2019 to 2022 seasons, with shoulder injuries classified by type and severity (games missed). Injury rates were calculated per 1000 athletic exposures using a one-game-per-athlete rule, and playoff games were excluded. Positions were compared with ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis and t-tests.
paper.findings: There were 452 shoulder injuries in 360 players, an injury rate of 4.5 per 1000 athletic exposures. Muscular/tendinous injuries were 40.9% (185) and ligamentous injuries 37.4% (169), and fractures were 1.3% (6). Fractures and ligamentous injuries were significantly more severe than muscular/tendinous and other injuries, and week 17 had the highest mean count with no overall seasonal trend.
paper.limitations: The data came from media and public compilations, which may contain reporting discrepancies and vague injury labels. Only the 2019 to 2022 seasons were included, the design is descriptive and cannot show causes, and yearly counts differ slightly between tables (2020 appears as 129, 130 and 131 across the text and tables).
paper.practicalImplications: Shoulder injuries are common in NFL players and mostly mild, but they still cost games on average. The authors suggest rotator cuff strengthening, gradual training-load progression, proper equipment fit and a deidentified injury registry to guide prevention.
paper.athleteDev: Position-specific shoulder work may suit linebackers, cornerbacks and wide receivers, who had the highest shoulder injury counts, with gradual load progression as the authors suggest. Read the counts as a prompt to look at each position's demands, not as a measure of individual risk.
paper.rtp: This study cannot guide return-to-play decisions because it reports injury counts and games missed, not recovery criteria, rehabilitation or re-injury outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Single nucleotide polymorphisms and tendon-ligament injuries in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Fukuyama Y, Murakami H, Iemitsu M. Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms and Tendon/Ligament Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: The review aimed to identify associations between genetic polymorphisms and tendon and ligament injuries in adolescent and adult athletes of multiple sports. It included 31 articles and identified 144 candidate polymorphisms, and the meta-analysis of 12 articles (1,687 injury cases and 2,227 controls) covered COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722, MMP3 rs679620 and VEGFA rs699947. Only VEGFA rs699947 was associated with injury, with the C allele linked to a lower risk (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.98).
paper.tldr: One gene variant (VEGFA rs699947, C allele) was linked to about 20% lower tendon and ligament injury risk in athletes, based on four studies. The other candidate variants showed no clear link, so genetic screening for these injuries is not supported yet.
paper.methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020, searching PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCO, Cochrane Library and MEDLINE to 7 July 2023 for genetic association studies of tendon or ligament injury in athletes. Study quality was rated with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and pooled odds ratios used DerSimonian and Laird random-effects models.
paper.findings: Of 144 candidate polymorphisms in 31 studies, four were pooled. For VEGFA rs699947, the C allele versus A allele gave OR 0.80 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.98, p = 0.03, I2 = 3.82%), while the dominant (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.18, I2 = 51.9%) and recessive (OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.12) models were not significant. COL1A1 rs1800012, COL5A1 rs12722 and MMP3 rs679620 showed no significant effect in any genetic model.
paper.limitations: The VEGFA finding rests on four studies, and few candidate-gene studies met meta-analysis criteria. The mechanisms of several variants are unclear, many studies came from one region so ethnic comparisons are limited, and competitive level, training time and nutrition were not accounted for.
paper.practicalImplications: Genetic variants are not yet usable to identify athletes at risk of tendon or ligament injury. The VEGFA result needs replication in larger samples before any practical use.
paper.athleteDev: This review cannot inform athlete development or training choices, since it covers injury association only. Genotype-based selection or program design is not supported by these findings.
paper.rtp: Cannot guide return to sport: the review compares injured and uninjured athletes and gives no information on rehabilitation, recovery or return timelines.

records.sourceFile: Sleep Disturbances and Risk of Sports Injury Among Collegiate Student-Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Messman BA, Petrie KA, Moore EWG, Petrie TA. Sleep Disturbances and Risk of Sports Injury Among Collegiate Student-Athletes. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: This secondary analysis of a national US survey of NCAA student-athletes compared 89 injured athletes with 89 exact-matched noninjured athletes across October 2020 and January 2021. Higher sleep disturbance in October 2020 was associated with higher odds of injury in January 2021 (OR 1.07 per unit, P = 0.007).
paper.tldr: In this matched sample of collegiate athletes, higher sleep disturbance scores in October 2020 were associated with higher odds of injury 3 months later. Sleep screening may be a reasonable part of athlete health monitoring, but this is an association from self-reported data.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of 178 student-athletes from a longitudinal US survey: 89 who reported injury in January 2021 and 89 noninjured matches (83 pairs matched on all 5 demographics, 6 on 4). Sleep disturbance was measured with the PROMIS Sleep Disturbance Short Form at both timepoints, and injury was self-reported. Analyses used a 2 x 3 repeated-measures ANOVA and a logistic regression of January injury on October sleep disturbance, adjusted for sport in-season, gender, race, ethnicity and October 2020 injury status.
paper.findings: Athletes injured in January 2021 had higher sleep disturbance scores than matched controls in October 2020 (M 54.77 vs 50.47) and January 2021 (M 54.41 vs 50.46). Athletes injured in October 2020 did not differ significantly from either group. The final model, which included October sleep disturbance, correctly classified 77.5% of January injury status, and the estimated January injury probability rose from 13% in the none-to-slight range to 26% to 33% in the mild to severe ranges.
paper.limitations: Injury and sleep were self-reported, and the sleep measure is a questionnaire rather than a clinical assessment. The sample was mostly female, White and non-Hispanic, and few athletes reached severe sleep disturbance, so effects in clinical populations may be larger or different. The 3-month gap and matched design cannot establish causation, and the authors note the unexpected lack of a sleep-injury link for athletes injured in October 2020.
paper.practicalImplications: Sleep disturbance could be included in routine athlete health screening, with referral when sleep complaints appear, as the authors recommend. The results support sleep as one possible injury-risk signal to follow up, not a validated threshold for changing training.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff could add a brief sleep disturbance check to routine athlete monitoring, since higher October scores preceded injury in this sample. Use a high score as a prompt for a conversation and follow-up, not as a reason to change load on its own.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It did not measure recovery or re-injury after return, and athletes injured in October 2020 did not differ significantly from the other groups on sleep.

records.sourceFile: Specificity and Areas of Usage of Cardiovascular Prediction Models Among Athletes—State-of-the-art Review.pdf

paper.citation: Chomiuk T, Kasiak P, Mamcarz A, Śliż D. Specificity and Areas of Usage of Cardiovascular Prediction Models Among Athletes, State-of-the-art Review. Rev Cardiovasc Med. 2025;26(5):37493.
paper.abstract: Summarizes the practical use of common prediction models for maximal oxygen uptake, cardiac arrhythmias, hypertension, atherosclerosis and cardiomyopathies in athletes, with a focus on endurance disciplines. The authors also propose a pre-participation protocol for applying these models.
paper.tldr: Cardiovascular risk models can help decide which athletes need a fuller medical check before progressive training. The authors present them as a screening aid rather than a diagnosis, and most have not been validated in athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative state-of-the-art review. No systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal are described.
paper.findings: The authors summarize atrial fibrillation scores (CHARGE-AF was judged most suitable for preliminary screening in European populations), Framingham-based hypertension scores and exercise blood pressure regression equations, and coronary artery disease models. They note that hypertension is more common in strength than endurance disciplines and that AF prevalence in middle-aged and master athletes has been reported at 12% to 29%. They recommend adding VO2max and other fitness indicators to future models.
paper.limitations: Narrative design with no described search method. Most models come from general populations, many lack external validation in athletes, and the authors identify gaps in ethnic and non-European representation. Several recommendations are described as preliminary.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a validated risk score as a first-pass screen to flag athletes who need a full clinical evaluation before intense or progressive training. Do not treat a score as a diagnosis, and recognize that most scores have not been validated in athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Risk and exercise-capacity screening can help set safe training intensity zones for amateur, master and professional endurance athletes, with a medical referral when risk is flagged.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review touches on return-to-play guidance for athletes with confirmed or suspected cardiovascular disease, but it gives no outcome data on return timelines. It cannot set a return-to-play decision alone and depends on the treating physician's assessment.

records.sourceFile: Spikes in acute-chronic workload ration associated with a 5-7 times greater injury rate in English Premier League football players - A comprehensive 3-year study.pdf

paper.citation: Bowen L, Gross AS, Gimpel M, Bruce-Low S, Li FX. Spikes in acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) associated with a 5-7 times greater injury rate in English Premier League football players: a comprehensive 3-year study. Br J Sports Med. 2020;54:731-738.
paper.abstract: Examined the relation between GPS-derived workloads and injury in 33 English Premier League players over three seasons. Cumulative loads and acute:chronic workload ratios were classified by z-scores and relative risk was calculated for injured versus non-injured players. Non-contact injury risk was highest when chronic exposure was low and the ACWR exceeded 2.0. The authors recommend monitoring the ACWR and avoiding spikes that approach or exceed 2.0.
paper.tldr: In this one-club study, sudden jumps in training load (ACWR above 2.0) on top of low chronic load were linked to the highest non-contact injury risk. The authors recommend building chronic load gradually and avoiding spikes near 2.0.
paper.methods: Analysis of GPS workload (StatSports Viper units, video-based match data from 2015/16) and club-recorded injury data over three seasons. Cumulative 1- to 4-week loads and ACWR were classified by z-scores, relative risks were estimated with binary logistic regression, and only conditions with 20 or more injuries were analysed.
paper.findings: For all injuries, a low chronic load of accelerations, decelerations or low-intensity distance combined with a very high ACWR gave RR 2.8 to 3.5. For non-contact injuries, a very high ACWR with low chronic load gave RR 4.5 (total distance) to 6.6 (decelerations), and with all chronic loads the very high ACWR gave RR 3.7 to 3.9. Overall injury risk with a very high ACWR across all chronic loads was RR 2.4 to 2.6. Contact injuries were linked to moderate to high ACWR (RR 2.0 to 2.6), and 80% of contact injuries occurred in matches.
paper.limitations: The abstract gives RR 6.7 for ACWR above 2.0 with low decelerations, while the results text and Table 5 give RR 6.6 at ACWR above 2.3; the abstract and text should be read together. The title range of 5 to 7 times rests on subgroup results, and the lowest value for total distance is 4.5. Other limits: 2014/15 match data were estimated, 11% of sessions were imputed, 61 player-seasons were treated as independent, sub-threshold injury cells were dropped, and only external load was measured.
paper.practicalImplications: Track the ACWR alongside cumulative load and avoid week-to-week spikes that approach or exceed 2.0, especially when chronic load is low. Build chronic load progressively, because the authors note that reducing load to lower risk can also cost fitness.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Use weekly GPS load and ACWR to plan progressions for squad members, avoiding spikes near 2.0 and building chronic load gradually before match-level demands.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not address return to play. Its ACWR thresholds describe in-season injury risk in healthy squad players and cannot set loading after an injury.

records.sourceFile: Sport Hernias - A comprehensive review for clinicians.pdf

paper.citation: Kopscik M, Crisman JL, Lomasney L, Smith S, Jadidi S. Sports Hernias: A Comprehensive Review for Clinicians. Cureus. 2023;15(8):e43283.
paper.abstract: Reviews current knowledge on sports hernias, a cause of chronic groin pain in athletes, covering pathogenesis, diagnostic approaches and management. The authors argue that the condition needs a multidisciplinary approach and further research.
paper.tldr: Sports hernia is a clinical diagnosis of chronic groin pain in athletes, and no single imaging study rules it out. Nonoperative rehabilitation is tried first, and surgery is considered when it fails after about three months.
paper.methods: Narrative clinical review. No search strategy, databases or inclusion criteria are described.
paper.findings: The authors describe men as more than 90% of cases, with soccer the most common sport. They report that a diagnosis is made when at least three of five examination signs are present, that MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality, and that the posterior inguinal wall was deficient in 85% of surgical cases in one cited study. Nonoperative care is a rest period of six to eight weeks followed by about six weeks of graded rehabilitation, and full return to sport is given as four to 12 weeks depending on the type of surgery and individual recovery.
paper.limitations: Narrative design with no described search, so the evidence base is not transparent. The authors state that dynamic ultrasound has low sensitivity and specificity, that the benefit of targeted strengthening for prevention is not established, and that prospective randomized surgical studies are needed. Return-to-play figures come from selected case series.
paper.practicalImplications: Make the diagnosis clinically from the examination signs, using imaging (MRI is the most sensitive) mainly to exclude other causes of groin pain. Start with rest and graded rehabilitation, and consider a surgical opinion if symptoms persist beyond about three months.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Athletes with groin pain need early assessment for a sports hernia so that core and hip adductor work can be planned; the review says the evidence that targeted strengthening prevents sports hernias is lacking.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The 4- to 12-week range after surgery and the staged nonoperative rehabilitation sequence can frame expectations. The reported return rates come from selected surgical and professional groups, and the review gives no criteria for individual clearance.
